cover.html:
- Thesis: the value is not the data, it is how fast a question becomes an answer and a signal becomes an action.
- Set expectations: about twelve minutes of framing, then we drive the live system.
- Say plainly: the feed is public aircraft data, and it stands in for whatever moves in their world.
problem.html:
- 17.2 million position reports in seven days, on one small demo. Nobody read them.
- The bottleneck is attention and time to answer, not storage.
- Ask the room: how long does it currently take to answer 'what was near this site last Tuesday'? Let the silence work.
- Avoid volume bragging; the point is the gap between arrival and use.
analogue.html:
- Everything that follows is a position, a time and an identity. Aircraft are just the honest public example.
- Name the domains that fit the people in the room: maritime, fleet, incidents, sensors.
- ASK: which of these four is closest to your feed? Use their answer for the rest of the session.
- Do not promise integrations here; the claim is about the pattern.
flow.html:
- Let the animation land before speaking; it draws five steps in about three seconds.
- Walk it once: positions arrive, place is attached, a shared picture forms, people ask or get briefed, urgent signals go to triage.
- This is the whole deck in one slide. Everything after it is a close-up on one hop.
- Deliberately no product names, no plumbing. If asked how it ingests, say 'a scheduled pull from an API' and move on.
live-picture.html:
- This one is a schematic, not a screenshot. Say so if asked, then show the real thing in Kibana.
- Teal is movement density, so busy areas summarise rather than smear. The thin lines are live tracks.
- The pulsing marks are objects signalling an emergency, on the same canvas as everything else.
- The value word is 'shared': one picture, so the room stops arguing about whose spreadsheet is right.
- DEMO: Aircraft World Overview dashboard. Zoom the globe, then point out the emergency markers.
context.html:
- Left is what the object broadcasts. Right is what gets stored, every single time.
- Country, region, nearest site and distance are attached on the way in, not looked up afterwards.
- Payoff: questions can be asked in plain geography, so nobody needs coordinates or a GIS specialist.
- If pressed on how: boundaries and site polygons are matched at ingest. Do not go deeper.
drill.html:
- Situational awareness is worthless if the detail lives in another system.
- Three scales, same screen: everything, an area, one object.
- Stress the audit angle: the trail from overview to underlying record stays intact, which matters for anything that ends up in a report or a court.
- DEMO: click through from the world map to Aircraft Detail for a single aircraft.
explore.html:
- The question is typed in plain English. No query language, no ticket to a data team.
- Read the three findings out; they are the kind of thing an analyst would want flagged.
- Value line: the people who understand the problem can now interrogate the data themselves.
- Governance question will come: answer that it runs under the same permissions as the user, and every answer cites its records.
- DEMO: AI Agents, tracking specialist. Ask about a region the room cares about.
journey.html:
- SKIPPABLE if short of time; live-picture and triage carry the argument.
- One question, thirty days, whole story: movements, ownership, current position, prior interest.
- 'Prior interest' is the one to dwell on: has anyone in the organisation already looked at this? That is the question that usually cannot be answered today.
- DEMO: ask the agent for an aircraft history report on a specific ICAO24.
site.html:
- SKIPPABLE if short of time.
- Note the caption: the same question works for a port, depot, hospital or substation.
- The hourly profile is the point. Once normal is visible, abnormal announces itself; no model required.
- The '12 with no known operator' line is the investigative hook.
- DEMO: ask the agent for airport activity around a named site.
briefing.html:
- Posted at 08:00 into the channel the team already reads. Nobody has to remember to run anything.
- Written from the data each morning, not a fixed template with the numbers swapped.
- It is also conversational: you can ask it follow-up questions in the same place.
- DEMO: show yesterday's briefing in Slack, then ask the briefing agent to expand a section.
watchlist.html:
- SKIPPABLE if short of time.
- Demo list is airlines that no longer exist. If a live aircraft still identifies as one, someone should know why.
- Be honest about what a match is: a lead, not a verdict. Usually stale equipment or a reassigned identifier.
- Then land the transfer: swap in vessels of interest, sanctioned operators, expired licences, plant reported stolen. The mechanism is unchanged.
- Keep aviation trivia out of the room; it is a watch-list story.
signal.html:
- 7500 is the code for a hijack in progress. Say it once, plainly, and let it sit.
- Counts are from seven days of live global data: 107, 93, 282.
- The tension: rare enough to be ignored, serious enough that it never can be. Most are equipment or human error, and somebody still has to establish which.
- DEMO: the emergency squawk panel on the World Overview dashboard.
triage.html:
- Walk the five steps once, no more: detect, check, gather, assess, hand over.
- 'Check' is the unglamorous one that people recognise: one incident stays one case however many alerts arrive.
- Under two minutes, and nobody had to be awake for it.
- This is the slide that usually earns the follow-up meeting. Slow down here.
- DEMO: open a real case created by the hijack investigation and scroll its attachments.
analyst.html:
- Read the verdict and the four reasons. Note it argues for a false alarm, and says so with moderate confidence.
- Every line links back to the record it came from. No unsourced assertions.
- The important sentence: it proposes, a person decides. Accountability and the record stay where they belong.
- Expect the AI governance question here. Answer: no autonomous action, reasoning is recorded, a human closes the case.
your-data.html:
- Turn it round: what they bring, what they get.
- 'Your definition of interesting' is the honest ask. That is the conversation we want, not a data dump.
- Data residency line matters in this room: own tenancy, UK region, own network, or own hardware.
- ASK: which of the four outcomes on the right would change a week in their operation?
recap.html:
- See, place, explore, act. Four jobs, one place.
- Callback to the flow slide; do not re-explain the architecture.
- Land the last line: no hand-offs between four tools, four copies of the data and four teams.
- Keep this short. The room should be impatient for the demo by now.
close.html:
- Hand over to the live system. Everything shown is running now on public data.
- Use the three 'bring' prompts to get a real question out of the room before opening Kibana.
- If nobody bites, start with the emergency panel; the 7500 story always restarts the conversation.
- Close with a concrete next step: a working session on one of their feeds.
